analysis.one_liner: Transfers the U.S. Postal Service to a private, employee-owned corporation.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and died in a House committee without ever getting a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have moved the entire U.S. Postal Service—its buildings, trucks, network, and legal powers—into a new private corporation. Postal employees would elect up to nine incorporators and receive stock in the company based on their years of service; after one year, that stock could be sold to the general public. A commission appointed mostly by the President would manage the handover, and the new corporation would keep the legal mail monopoly (the 'private express statutes') for its first five years. The House committee that handles postal matters never acted on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The new private postal corporation and, eventually, its shareholders. Employees get an initial stake, but the one-year window for employee-only shares means ownership can shift to public investors, and the corporation inherits all Postal Service assets plus a five-year continuation of the legal monopoly on first-class mail delivery.
analysis.who_benefits_short: A new private mail corporation and its shareholders

how_it_helps.text: All right, title, and interest of the United States in Postal Service property would be transferred to a private corporation.

Postal employees would elect up to nine qualified incorporators and receive securities issued only to employees for the first year, allocated by years of service and compensation, with retirement benefits comparable to their federal ones.
After the first year, the corporation's securities could be offered for sale to the general public on terms the corporation itself considers appropriate.
The President's transfer plan could include continuing the private express statutes—the legal monopoly on ordinary mail delivery—for the corporation's first five years.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, who own the Postal Service's assets and would see them handed to a private corporation under a plan the President writes, and mail customers—especially in rural and high-cost areas—who would depend on a profit-seeking company (with only five years of monopoly protection and no guaranteed rate restraint after that) to keep universal service affordable.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and mail customers, especially rural ones

drawbacks.text: The bill requires the corporation only to include postal delivery consistent with the public-service purposes of title 39 among its purposes; it contains no mechanism guaranteeing universal service at affordable rates once the five-year monopoly protection and transitional rate arrangements end.

Employee ownership is temporary by design: after one year shares can be sold to the general public, so control of a former public asset could concentrate in outside investors within months of the transfer.
The President—not Congress—would determine when the corporation qualifies and would write the transfer plan and rate-setting proposals, leaving Congress only to receive recommendations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The employee-share plan and comparable retirement protections are real sweeteners, but the core of the bill is transferring a publicly owned network—built and financed by the public—to a private corporation, with the profits flowing to its shareholders and the pricing power largely protected for five years by a legal monopoly. Any risk to universal, affordable mail service would fall hardest on rural customers and low-income households. The House postal committee's lack of action suggests lawmakers on both sides saw the costs as outweighing the benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Post Office and Civil Service Committee and its postal subcommittees, never got a hearing or vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Philip Crane introduced the bill on February 28, 1989.

The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Post Office and Civil Service, and a week later split between two subcommittees—the Subcommittee on Postal Personnel and Modernization and the Subcommittee on Postal Operations and Services—with executive comment requested from OMB and the Postal Service.
No member signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nobody changed position because the bill never advanced: the Postal Service stayed a public agency, so mail customers—particularly rural ones—kept universal service under public control, and postal workers kept their public employer. The proposal had so little support (zero cosponsors) that its death changed little in practice.

for.name: Rep. Philip M. Crane
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to privatize the Postal Service; no other member joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Post Office and Civil Service
against.role: Committee of referral for all postal legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to two postal subcommittees and took no further action—no markup, no hearing, no vote—leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Rep. William D. Ford
against.role: Chair, House Post Office and Civil Service Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: This was never a party fight: one Republican introduced it, no member of either party cosponsored it, and there were no roll-call votes.

industries.note: The bill would hand the corporation every Postal Service asset and continue the private express statutes—the legal monopoly on ordinary mail—for its first five years, while rate-setting authority during that period would be shaped by presidential proposal rather than the existing independent Rate Commission after transition. Its gains would come from public assets and a protected market, not from outperforming a public agency on price.

Employees would receive company securities allocated by service and pay, with comparable retirement benefits, but they would exchange a public employer and public-employee status for shares that could be sold off and a company whose long-term treatment of labor the bill leaves to itself.

The corporation would start with a five-year mail monopoly, but privatization of the largest mail network would reshape competition for letters, parcels, and logistics—potentially opening markets later while facing a capitalized private rival built from the old monopoly's assets.
